column1: What are the three axioms defining a continuous-time flow $\phi^t: X \to X$?
column2: 1) Identity: $\phi^0 = \text{id}_X$. 2) Composition: $\phi^{t+s} = \phi^t \circ \phi^s$ for all $t,s \in \mathbb{R}$. 3) Continuity of $(t,x) \mapsto \phi^t(x)$ jointly in time and state. Together these make $\{\phi^t\}$ a one-parameter group of homeomorphisms/diffeomorphisms.

column1: Distinguish Lyapunov stability from asymptotic stability for an equilibrium $x^*$.
column2: Lyapunov stable: for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $\|x_0-x^*\|<\delta \implies \|\phi(t,x_0)-x^*\|<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge0$ (bounded, no convergence required). Asymptotic stability additionally requires $\lim_{t\to\infty}\phi(t,x_0)=x^*$. Example: undamped oscillator is Lyapunov stable but not asymptotically stable; damped oscillator is asymptotically stable.

column1: What common misconception does the undamped harmonic oscillator ($\ddot{x}+\omega^2x=0$) correct about stability?
column2: It shows Lyapunov stability does NOT imply asymptotic stability — nearby orbits (closed ellipses) stay bounded near the equilibrium forever but never converge to it.

column1: State the Hartman-Grobman theorem for discrete maps and its hyperbolicity condition.
column2: Near a fixed point $p$ with multiplier $\lambda=f'(p)$ satisfying $|\lambda|\neq 1$ (hyperbolic), $f$ is topologically conjugate to its linearization $x \mapsto \lambda x$. The case $|\lambda|=1$ is non-hyperbolic and requires higher-order (bifurcation) analysis.

column1: Define topological conjugacy between two discrete dynamical systems $(X,f)$ and $(Y,g)$.
column2: A homeomorphism $h: X \to Y$ exists such that $h \circ f = g \circ h$. Conjugacy preserves all topological dynamical properties: period lengths, orbit structure, and entropy — it is the fundamental equivalence relation for classifying systems.

column1: What two eigenvalue conditions on the Jacobian $D_xf(x_0,\mu_0)$ signal a bifurcation at a fixed point?
column2: A zero eigenvalue (steady-state/saddle-node type bifurcations) or a pair of purely imaginary eigenvalues (Hopf bifurcation). At these singularities the linearization fails to determine nonlinear behavior, requiring higher-order Taylor terms or center manifold reduction.

column1: What is the center manifold theorem's key simplification for bifurcation analysis?
column2: When the Jacobian has eigenvalues with zero real part (center subspace) alongside stable/unstable eigenvalues, the local dynamics reduce asymptotically to a low-dimensional flow on a center manifold tangent to the center eigenspace. The center manifold isn't unique, but all choices share the same Taylor expansion to all orders, and the reduced dynamics are equivalent.

column1: Give the formula for the maximal Lyapunov exponent $\lambda$ and its chaos criterion.
column2: $$\lambda = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}\ln\frac{\|\delta(t)\|}{\|\delta_0\|}$$ A positive $\lambda$ signals chaos: nearby trajectories diverge exponentially as $\|\delta(t)\| \sim \|\delta_0\|e^{\lambda t}$, implying measurement errors double every $(1/\lambda)\ln 2$ time units.

column1: What is the variational equation governing infinitesimal perturbation growth along a trajectory?
column2: $$\frac{d}{dt}\delta(t) = Df(\phi_t(x_0)) \cdot \delta(t)$$ where $Df$ is the Jacobian of the vector field evaluated along the trajectory; it linearizes the separation dynamics between nearby orbits.

column1: What three properties jointly formalize chaos (per the curriculum's three pillars)?
column2: 1) Topological transitivity (trajectories explore phase space densely). 2) Dense periodic orbits (periodic solutions populate the attractor densely). 3) Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (positive Lyapunov exponent causing exponential divergence).

column1: Define what it means for a measure $\mu$ to be invariant under a transformation $T: X \to X$.
column2: For every measurable set $A \in \mathcal{B}$: $\mu(T^{-1}(A)) = \mu(A)$. This means the statistical distribution of an ensemble initialized according to $\mu$ remains $\mu$ after evolving under $T$.

column1: State the Krylov-Bogolyubov theorem and sketch its proof mechanism.
column2: For any continuous map $T$ on a compact metric space, at least one $T$-invariant Borel probability measure exists. Proof: form Cesàro averages $\mu_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}T_*^k\nu$ of pushforwards of any initial measure $\nu$; weak-$*$ compactness of probability measures guarantees a convergent subsequence, and its limit is necessarily $T$-invariant.
